Pipeline overview

Five stages. Each stage reads saved files from earlier stages. The list below groups the notebooks into seven tasks. Cell numbers (tab 2) count from 0 in the .ipynb file.

Stage A · 11 notebooks

Housing price

Price per m² for every residential building (10,000 KRW/m²).
Stage B · 1 notebook

Population

WorldPop grid (3 arc-second, about 100 m) downscaled to buildings.
Stage C · 1 notebook

SEVI

Subdistrict SEVI by PCA, split to buildings by inverse price.
Stage D · 3 notebooks

Risk index

Hazard × exposure × vulnerability classes, building and subdistrict level.
Stage E · 3 notebooks

Follow-up analyses

Resource allocation, risk inside subdistricts, and flooded vs non-flooded buildings.

The principle

How each of H, E, V and R is formed. The hazard figure reads 1 → 2 → 3, for a real subdistrict (top row) and a real building (bottom row). The equations follow. H, E and V classes 1–5 are fifths: 5 means the top 20 % of the units ranked. R is rounded from them, so its classes are uneven.

H · Hazard

How much of the place floods, and how deep? Deeper water counts more: each depth band is weighted by the share of home contents a flood that deep destroys (Korean national damage rates, Jung et al. 2023).

3

Key assumptions & parameters

The choices and constants that shape the results, in run order.

Parameters by step

One card per step, in run order. One line per assumption. “Manuscript” = from the paper text.

Buildings and prices

Residential buildings

  • Source: 2025.12 building register, 7 districts
  • Type: from the register’s main-use text: row, detached, apartment, other

Addresses

  • Jeollanam: address found by reverse geocoding a point inside each footprint
  • Price join: on the lot address only

Prices to 2025

  • Index: Dec 2025 = 100; Gwangju apartments by gu, Jeollanam apartments one series, row and detached houses by province
  • Rent → sale: deposit-to-jeonse and jeonse-to-price ratios (REB, manuscript); the monthly payment is ignored
  • Detached match: kept if the floor areas differ by ≤ 5 m²
  • Dropped: jeonse records older than the ratio series

One price per building

  • Order: sale, then jeonse, then monthly rent
  • Several types: mean of them
  • Outliers: known prices outside the 1st–99th percentile dropped

Subdistrict price

  • Price: 2021 income × PIR (Gwangju 7.47, Jeollanam 5.19), brought to Dec 2025 with the index
  • Per m²: ÷ mean footprint area (stands in for floor area)
  • Floor: scaled up by α ≥ 1, set from the 20th percentile of known prices; 42 of 118 subdistricts raised

500 m grid

  • Known cell: ≥ 70 % of its buildings priced
  • β lower bound: 0.285; 256 of 3,045 cells sit at it

POI weights

  • Layers: 10 POI categories, one Thiessen layer each
  • Weight: |Pearson r| between TF-IDF and the grid value, scaled to sum to 1

People and vulnerability

Population

  • Source: WorldPop 2025, 3 arc-second cells
  • Merged: 진월동 and 신용동 counted in polygons 116 and 117
  • Correction: only outlier subdistricts rescaled (2022 ratios); none flagged after the merge
  • Empty polygons: their people go to the 10 nearest buildings, by 1/d
  • Open: k = 10 not confirmed (code comment: the user’s choice; fix report: a default)

Subdistrict SEVI

  • Merged: 효덕동 + 진월동 and 건국동 + 신용동 (each indicator weighted by its own denominator); 중흥3동 takes 중흥2동’s value
  • Indicators: 43 → 19 (18 in _261028): |r| > 0.9 or < 0.001 removed, P_40_64 removed by hand
  • PCA: 5 PCs (> 80 % variance), varimax; weights 0.487 / 0.203 / 0.125 / 0.119 / 0.066
  • Scale: 0.01–1, so the lowest subdistrict still splits across its buildings (not 0 for all)

Building SEVI

  • Weight: 1 / price, scaled so the building mean = the subdistrict SEVI
  • Assumption: higher price → higher income → lower vulnerability; the 0.01 floor lets every subdistrict be split this way

Flood and risk

Hazard

  • Event: one 100-year flood, floodmap.go.kr depth classes (manuscript)
  • Damage rate: 0.066 / 0.153 / 0.608 / 0.988 / 1.0 for < 0.5 / 0.5–1 / 1–2 / 2–5 / > 5 m
  • Building: damage-weighted flooded share of a 30 m circle; quintiles over 27,804
  • Subdistrict: damage-weighted flooded km²; quintiles over 96

Classes 1–5

  • E: quintiles over the 27,804 exposed buildings
  • V: quintiles over all 166,999 buildings, so exposed classes are uneven (4,578–6,801 each)
  • Why: E depends on the flood, V does not (same for subdistricts)

Risk index

  • Formula: R = \(\text{round}\left(\sqrt[3]{H\cdot E\cdot V}\right)\), both levels
  • Basis: adapted from \(\sqrt{E\cdot V}\) (manuscript)

Using the results

Allocation

  • Pool: all 27,804 exposed buildings
  • Target: Rb ≥ 4 (5,261 buildings)
  • Budget: every N from 1 to 27,804
  • Rules: subdistrict-based, building-based and hybrid (tab 5)

Heterogeneity

  • Split: variance of raw risk inside vs between subdistricts
  • LISA: raw building risk, k = 8 neighbours, 9,999 permutations, FDR q = 0.05
  • Checked: with k = 4 / 8 / 16, 24 / 29 / 33 % of hot spots sit in subdistricts rated 1–3, so the finding holds; k = 8 is the original author’s value and follows Esri’s rule of thumb of at least eight neighbours (ArcGIS Pro, Modeling spatial relationships; used by Khan et al. 2017, Spat. Spatio-temporal Epidemiol. 21:67–75)

Building vs subdistrict: three results

The same flood, rated building by building and subdistrict by subdistrict. Open each result in turn.

Result 1 · how much

The two scales disagree, in both directions

Only about a third of flooded buildings share their subdistrict’s risk class; the rest sit above or below it.

real values Exposed buildings. Above each column: share (count) with Rb ≥ 4; n = buildings; inside: share of each Rb. One building without Rs left out. Data:
build_risk_class_261030_equal_sqrt.pkl

What it shows

  • Big picture: the two scales rate the same flood differently, so a subdistrict map both misses higher-risk buildings and includes lower-risk ones.
  • Same class for about a third: 35 % of flooded buildings share their subdistrict’s risk class; 12 % are rated higher and 53 % lower.
  • Two scales, two pictures: a third of the higher-risk buildings (1,768 of 5,261) stand in subdistricts rated medium or lower.
  • The reverse holds too: in subdistricts rated 4 or 5, only about a quarter of exposed buildings (3,493 of 12,916) are higher-risk (Fig. 10).
  • Why it matters: the two levels rank places differently, so a subdistrict rating can miss higher-risk buildings and include lower-risk ones.
  • Spread inside subdistricts: in this model, about two thirds of the variation in building risk lies inside subdistricts, and high-risk buildings cluster (tab 5, item 2).
Result 2 · why

Each error has its own cause

Missed buildings have higher local hazard and vulnerability than their area; over-included ones have lower local hazard and exposure.

Fig. 11. What sets a building apart from its subdistrict: (a) missed buildings (Rb ≥ 4 in subdistricts rated 1–3); (b) over-included buildings (Rb ≤ 3 in subdistricts rated 4–5)

real values 1,768 missed and 9,423 over-included buildings (result 1). A part counts when the building’s own class is above (missed) or below (over-included) its subdistrict’s. Data:
build_risk_class_261030_equal_sqrt.pkl
dong_risk_261030_equal_sqrt[3].pkl

What it shows

  • Big picture: a subdistrict rating describes the area as a whole, so it misses buildings in deeper water that are more vulnerable than their area, and includes buildings in shallower water with lower exposure.
  • Missed buildings: their own hazard is above their area’s in 74 % and their own vulnerability in 80 %; exposure shows no pattern (30 % above, 32 % below).
  • Over-included buildings: their own hazard is below their area’s in 79 % and their own exposure in 76 %; vulnerability shows no pattern.
  • Why the scales differ: a subdistrict’s hazard and exposure add up its whole flooded area and all its flooded residents, so they rate the area, not each building’s water and residents.
Result 3 · on the ground

One rating, many building risks

Four subdistricts, building by building: missed, over-included, both ways, and agreement.

real values Flooded footprints by own risk class, in each subdistrict’s most flooded 400 m square (above / below shares within 9 points of the whole area). Areas: the clearest case of each type, chosen from the data. Flood: 100-year depth (Flood_area.shp). Basemap: Esri World Street Map (Esri, TomTom, Garmin, FAO, NOAA, USGS, © OpenStreetMap contributors, GIS User Community). Data:

What it shows

  • Big picture: missed buildings sit in deeper water and are more vulnerable than their area; over-included buildings sit in shallower water and have lower exposure (basin-wide, result 2).
  • Missed: Baegun 2(i) is rated 3, yet 164 of its 391 flooded buildings (42 %) are higher-risk.
  • Over-included: Unam 2(i) is rated 4, yet 708 of its 926 (76 %) are not higher-risk.
  • Both ways: Wolsan 4(sa) is rated 3; 179 of its 703 are rated higher and 137 lower.
  • Agreement: Hwajeong 2(i) is rated 4, and 230 of its 419 (55 %) are higher-risk.
5

Results analysis

The supervisor’s follow-up analyses. Open each one below.

Item 1 · Resource allocation

Who to support

Selecting buildings by their own risk captures far more higher-risk buildings for the same budget than selecting subdistricts, and organising delivery by subdistrict keeps the work compact.

Item 2 · Flood risk heterogeneity

Why building level, and where the pockets are

Most flood risk varies inside subdistricts, and high-risk buildings cluster, including in pockets the area map rates lower. Local measures placed at these clusters could cover many high-risk buildings at once.

Item 3 · Flooded and non-flooded

Where vulnerability and flood overlap

The 100-year flood takes in only slightly more vulnerable buildings than its share (46 % vs 40 % in the two most vulnerable classes), mostly in the more vulnerable of the large, rural subdistricts; in small subdistricts there is no gap.

Items 1, 2 and 3

What the analyses show together

The subdistrict scale hides where flood risk sits, so area-based selection would miss some higher-risk buildings and include lower-risk ones.

  1. The cause: about two thirds (68 %) of the variation in building flood risk lies inside subdistricts; a subdistrict rating can show only the other third.
  2. Hidden risk: 34 % of higher-risk buildings (1,768 of 5,261) and 29 % of buildings in high-risk clusters (1,323 of 4,563) sit in subdistricts rated 1–3.
  3. Errors both ways: lower-rated subdistricts hold many higher-risk buildings (Juwol 2(i), rated 3: 286), while some high-rated ones hold few (Geonguk, rated 5: 39 of 229).
  4. Budget: for the same budget (5,000 buildings), selecting by building risk captures 95 % of higher-risk buildings, against 33 % by subdistrict.
  5. Vulnerability and flood: vulnerable buildings are slightly over-represented in the flood extent (46 % vs 40 %), and the gap lies in the large, rural subdistricts, where flooded buildings sit in the more vulnerable ones (no gap in small ones); inside subdistricts there is no consistent pattern.
  6. Delivery: choosing by building risk and then ordering by subdistrict captures as many higher-risk buildings in about a quarter fewer subdistricts (57 vs 76).

Decision rule: decide who gets support by building risk; organise delivery by subdistrict or cluster; keep area-wide measures (e.g. warnings, evacuation help) for subdistricts with high exposure or where vulnerability and flood overlap.

Limits: counts are buildings, not people; no cost data, so lower delivery cost is an implication; hot-spot shares depend on the neighbourhood size; building H, E and V rest on the model’s downscaling assumptions.

Supervisor item 1 · notebook _261031

Resource allocation

Same budget, three ways to target it: how many higher-risk buildings each captures, and how many subdistricts the work spans.

What the supervisor asked

Prof. DK, item 1 (Feedbacks_Prof.DK_260625.docx): compare three targeting approaches under a fixed budget.

Set-up

  • Budget: same number of buildings for all, e.g. 1,000 / 5,000 / 10,000
  • Subdistrict-based: pick subdistricts by Rs
  • Building-based: pick buildings by Rb
  • Hybrid: pick subdistricts by Rs, then buildings inside by Rb
  • Our change: the hybrid ranks Rb first, then Rs, so it misses no higher-risk building

Measures and purpose

  • Capture = share of all higher-risk buildings that are selected
  • Precision = share of selected buildings that are higher-risk
  • Counted as (asked): buildings, residents, and V × residents
  • Our change: buildings only. This is a building-level assessment, and our data do not support a reliable count of people.
  • Our addition: subdistricts to work in
  • Purpose: how much does subdistrict-only targeting miss?

Answered here: every budget N from 1 to 27,804 (includes 1,000 / 5,000 / 10,000). Result figure = buildings.

Method: three ways to spend the same budget

Each approach picks 6 buildings from the same toy area.

Toy area: same input for all three

Subdistrict-based

Building-based

Hybrid

\[\text{Capture}(N)=\frac{\sum_{i\in S_N} w_i\,[R_{b,i}\ge 4]}{\sum_{i} w_i\,[R_{b,i}\ge 4]}\]Share of all targets that the N selected buildings SN include.
\[\text{Precision}(N)=\frac{\sum_{i\in S_N} w_i\,[R_{b,i}\ge 4]}{\sum_{i\in S_N} w_i}\]Share of the selection that is a target.

wi = 1 (buildings), residents, or Vclass × residents. Subdistricts to work in = subdistricts with at least one selected building; fewer means less coordination. All are computed for every budget N.

Result: same budget, different capture and spread

A third of the higher-risk buildings sit in subdistricts rated 3 or lower (map in tab 4). Ranking buildings first captures them; adding Rs keeps the work in fewer subdistricts.

What the results say

  • Area ratings hide risk: about a third of higher-risk buildings sit in areas rated lower, so funding the top-rated areas first leaves them out.
  • Area ratings also spend on lower risk: some high-rated areas hold few higher-risk buildings (in Geonguk, rated 5, 39 of 229), so area funding also goes to lower-risk buildings.
  • Higher capture per budget: funding buildings by their own risk captures two to three times as many higher-risk buildings as funding by subdistrict, most at small budgets.
  • Same capture, simpler delivery: choosing buildings by risk and then organising the work by subdistrict captures just as many in about a quarter fewer subdistricts. Fewer subdistricts to coordinate could lower delivery cost.
  • For budget decisions: decide who gets support by building risk; organise the work by subdistrict.
Supervisor item 2 · notebook _261031

Flood risk heterogeneity within subdistricts

Does one subdistrict risk class hide how flood risk differs and clusters among its buildings?

What the supervisor asked

Prof. DK, item 2 (Feedbacks_Prof.DK_260625.docx): show what a single subdistrict score hides.

Asked

  • How mixed: Shannon entropy of building vulnerability classes, per subdistrict
  • How clustered: Local Moran’s I per building; hot spots, cold spots and outliers counted per subdistrict
  • Purpose: tell subdistricts with many vulnerable buildings from those where they group together
  • Link: explain the subdistrict maps (Figs. 10–12)

Our choices

  • Scope: flood risk of the 27,804 flood-exposed buildings
  • Input: each building’s raw risk ∛(H·E·V); the 1–5 risk classes only as a check
  • Chance hits: false-discovery-rate correction (q = 0.05), 9,999 permutations
  • Neighbours: 8 nearest exposed buildings; 4 and 16 as a check
  • How mixed: share of the risk spread inside subdistricts (variance)
  • Not used: Shannon entropy
  • Not reported: vulnerability alone; inside a subdistrict, building SEVI differs only by housing price, so its spread is built in

Method: does risk vary inside a subdistrict, and does it cluster?

The subdistrict map gives each subdistrict one risk class. Two sets of buildings can share that class and still look very different inside.

Fig. A1. Three toy subdistricts with the same subdistrict risk class

\[\sum_i (r_i-\bar r)^2=\sum_s n_s(\bar r_s-\bar r)^2+\sum_s\sum_{i\in s}(r_i-\bar r_s)^2\]Variance split: how much risk varies inside subdistricts
Left: total spread of risk over all exposed buildings
First sum: between subdistricts (how far subdistrict averages differ)
Second sum: inside subdistricts (how far buildings differ from their own subdistrict’s average)
ri = raw risk ∛(H·E·V) of exposed building i; r̄s = average of subdistrict s; r̄ = average of all; ns = exposed buildings in s
Inside share = 68 %; between share = 32 %, the only part a subdistrict map can show
\[I_i=z_i\sum_{j\in N_8(i)} w_{ij}\,z_j\]LISA (Local Moran’s I): how clustered, building by building
Ii = Local Moran’s I of building i: above 0 = like its neighbours, below 0 = unlike them
zi, zj = raw risk ∛(H·E·V) of building i and of neighbour j, standardised (0 = mean of exposed buildings)
N8(i) = the 8 nearest exposed buildings to i
wij = weight of neighbour j, 1/8 each
Hot spot = zi > 0 and Ii > 0 (high among high), significant after FDR (q = 0.05, 9,999 permutations)

Result: the area map misses about three in ten risk hot-spot buildings

27,804 flood-exposed buildings in 92 subdistricts; hot spots tested on each building’s raw risk with 8 neighbours, 9,999 permutations and FDR (q = 0.05).

Check, neighbours: exposed buildings in hot spots with 4 / 8 / 16 neighbours: 7.7 / 16.4 / 22.2 %; 78 % (4) and 80 % (16) keep their k = 8 label. Hot spots in subdistricts rated 1–3: 24 / 29 / 33 %, so the main finding holds. Neighbours are the nearest exposed buildings, so they can be far apart where few buildings flood.
Check, classes: the 1–5 risk classes find 3,392 hot-spot buildings; 85 % of buildings get the same label as with the raw score.

What the results say

  • Risk varies most inside areas: about two thirds of the difference in flood risk lies between buildings of the same subdistrict.
  • High-risk buildings cluster: about one in six flood-exposed buildings is a hot spot (the share depends on the neighbourhood size).
  • The area map misses about three in ten: 1,323 of these buildings lie in subdistricts rated 1–3; Juwol 2(i), rated 3, holds 297.
  • A high rating is not high risk everywhere: Geonguk, rated 5, has only 18 such buildings among 229 exposed; its rating comes from many exposed residents (5,615) in large buildings (about 25 residents each), which still calls for area-wide measures such as evacuation planning, not blanket building support.
  • For research: in this basin and model, most variation in flood risk lies between buildings of the same subdistrict, which an area index cannot show.
  • For decision makers: plan flood protection around building-level risk clusters; area ratings alone would rank about three in ten of their buildings as lower priority.
Supervisor item 3 · notebook _261031b

Vulnerability in flooded and non-flooded buildings

Are flooded, or more deeply flooded, buildings more vulnerable?

What the supervisor asked

Prof. DK, item 3 (Feedbacks_Prof.DK_260625.docx): compare vulnerability inside and outside the flood extent.

Asked

  • Compare: flooded and non-flooded buildings, basin-wide and per subdistrict
  • Measures: mean or median vulnerability, share of highly vulnerable buildings; also population-weighted (V × population) where possible
  • Purpose: does the 100-year extent disproportionately include vulnerable buildings? Not: does flooding move vulnerable people
  • Tests: Mann–Whitney, KS or permutation “if needed”

Our choices

  • Unit: buildings (166,999), not people
  • Flooded: the 27,804 flood-exposed buildings used for risk; the other 139,195 are not flooded
  • Compare shares, not counts: the groups differ about fivefold in size
  • Extent: share of buildings in vulnerability classes 4–5, flooded vs the whole basin (representation ratio)
  • Depth: rank correlation of flood hazard class and SEVI at both levels, with a subdistrict-size check
  • Inference: effect sizes, subdistrict-resampling intervals and a within-subdistrict permutation test
  • Per subdistrict: where both groups have at least 30 buildings (74 subdistricts)

Keep in mind: building SEVI = subdistrict SEVI split by housing price, so inside a subdistrict the comparison is a housing-price comparison.

Method: two questions, two measures

Extent: does the flood extent hold more vulnerable buildings than its share? Depth: are more deeply flooded buildings and subdistricts more vulnerable?

The two questions, on toy buildings

\[\rho=\frac{p_{\mathrm{fl}}}{p_{\mathrm{all}}}\]Representation ratio: does the flood hold more vulnerable buildings than its share?
pfl = share of flooded buildings in vulnerability classes 4–5
pall = the same share among all buildings in the basin
ρ above 1 = vulnerable buildings over-represented; 1 = in proportion
\[r_s=\operatorname{corr}\left(\operatorname{rank}H,\ \operatorname{rank}V\right)\]Rank correlation: does vulnerability rise with flood hazard?
H = flood hazard class 1–5 (building: 30 m circle; subdistrict: damage-weighted flooded area in km²)
V = SEVI of the building (0.002–6.8), or of the subdistrict (0.01–1)
rs runs from −1 to 1; 0 = no relation
Size check: subdistrict H counts km², so rs is also computed with subdistrict size held fixed

Result: in this flood, vulnerability and flooding are only weakly related

166,999 buildings, 27,804 flooded; 91 subdistricts with a hazard class. Intervals from 2,000 resamples of whole subdistricts.

Fig. 16. The highest flood hazard sits in large, sparsely built subdistricts

real values Buildings. Large = over 10 km² (36 of 118 subdistricts; 35 of 91 with a hazard class). Fig. 16 shows buildings and subdistricts in hazard class 5. Data (Results\261031b\ in 5_Flooded_vs_nonflooded_Claude):
summary.csv
depth_summary.csv
depth_buildings_by_size.csv

build_risk_class_261030_equal_sqrt.pkl (hazard 5 buildings)

  • Where the gap comes from: the large, mostly rural subdistricts. There, 37 % of flooded buildings are vulnerable (classes 4–5) against 25 % of all their buildings (ratio 1.48). In the 82 small urban subdistricts there is no gap (54 % vs 54 %).
  • Inside subdistricts: no common direction. Flooded buildings are more vulnerable in 23 subdistricts, less in 25 and unclear in 26, and hazard is unrelated to SEVI (median rank correlation −0.02).
  • Size of the effect: small. Across the basin the ratio stays just above 1 (1.02–1.28; Cliff’s delta 0.09).
  • Housing price: flooded buildings are not cheaper (median price ratio 0.99).
  • Compared with Seoul: there, recorded floods (2010–2022) fell mostly in lower-price areas (Vuong Tai et al., 2025); here the 100-year flood shows only a slight tilt. Flood type, unit (basements vs all buildings) and measure (income vs SEVI) differ.

What the results say

  • The 100-year flood takes in vulnerable and less vulnerable buildings almost equally: in towns, flooded buildings are as vulnerable as the rest; the small tilt across the basin lies in the countryside, where flooded buildings sit in the more vulnerable of the large, rural areas.
  • High hazard is not where vulnerability is highest: the highest flood hazard sits in large, mostly rural areas, where vulnerability is lower on average.
  • The flood map and the vulnerability map overlap only slightly: neither alone shows which buildings are most at risk.
  • For budget decisions: choose who gets support with the combined building risk rating (items 1 and 2), not with flood depth or vulnerability alone.

Expected limitations and intended choices

k = 10 nearest buildings

Leftover people go to the 10 nearest buildings; one gets up to 274 extra. k = 10 was chosen in the 28 Oct fix; the original author’s value is not known.

A subdistrict on a class edge

R is rounded at x.5. Closest: subdistricts 4, 99 and 110 are R 3 by 0.020; 29, 31 and 52 stay R 2 by 0.034.

Single return period

Only the 100-year flood (manuscript Limitation).

Ground-level population

No floors or units, so multi-storey buildings are not resolved (manuscript Limitation).

Price as an income proxy

Building V rests on housing price; PIR is province-level, for 2021.

Footprint for floor area

Subdistrict prices use footprint area, then the α correction.

2022 ratios reused for 2025

Small subdistricts

18 of 92 exposed subdistricts have fewer than 30 exposed buildings (3 have only one), so their within-subdistrict results are unstable.

Partly taken subdistrict

In the subdistrict-based rule the last subdistrict counts at its expected value; best and worst cases form a band in the notebook figures; tab 5 shows the expected value.

Quintile sets (intended)

E depends on the flood: cut over the 27,804 exposed buildings. V does not: cut over all 166,999.

Relative hazard classes (intended)

H is a quintile class at both levels, so H 5 means the top fifth, not a physical depth.

0.58 loading cut (intended)

Each indicator loads high on one PC; holds for the final 19 (MP 0.604, PPH −0.588). All loadings still enter SEVI.

API keys in the notebook (intended)

Literature on classing

How published studies turn hazard, exposure and vulnerability into classes and combine them into risk. Condensed from lit_review_classing_261029.md (2026-10-29).

At a glance

E and V quintiles have clear precedent. H was the odd one out: an absolute, averaged depth level combined with two relative quintiles through a rule that needs all three to be high together. Since _261030 H is a damage-weighted quintile at both levels.

Hazard: from depth zones to one value

Korean flood risk maps use five depth bands: ≤ 0.5, 0.5–1, 1–2, 2–5 and ≥ 5 m (). The rules below give one value per unit; an invented subdistrict shows how far apart they land.

How to resolve

  • Update the manuscript’s abstract, results and conclusion, Table 3 and the population text.
  • Update CLAUDE.md, the two analysis READMEs, and the markdown and printed interpretation in #18 (cells 1, 14, 20 title, 22–24) and #19.

Same class, very different places.

  • Finding: A subdistrict can be uniform, mixed at random, or hold a cluster of high-risk buildings, and its single class looks the same in all three.
  • Why it matters: Each case needs a different response, so the score alone cannot tell planners where or how to act.

The area map misses about three in ten risk hot-spot buildings.

  • Finding: 4,563 flood-exposed buildings form clusters of high risk; 1,323 of them (29 %) are in subdistricts rated 1–3, such as Juwol 2(i), rated 3, with 297.
  • Why it matters: A plan that follows area ratings would treat about three in ten buildings in the riskiest clusters as lower priority.

Why not Shannon entropy

  • What it measures: how evenly a subdistrict’s buildings spread over the five risk classes (0 = all in one class, 1 = equal shares).
  • Depends on the classes: it changes with where the five class cut-offs fall.
  • Unstable when small: it is biased low where a subdistrict has few exposed buildings (18 of 92 have fewer than 30).
  • Answers a side question: it says how mixed one subdistrict is, not how much a subdistrict map hides.
  • Used instead: the variance split in (b), one number for the share of risk spread inside subdistricts (68 %), with no classes and no small-sample bias.
  • Still computed: in the notebook (risk_by_dong.csv, column H_norm).

Risk clusters sit inside subdistricts.

  • Finding: high-risk buildings form clusters inside subdistricts of every rating. Juwol 1(il) holds the most (558); Juwol 2(i), rated 3, holds 297; Geonguk, rated 5, only 18.
  • Why it matters: a cluster is a natural unit for area-based measures, such as local drainage or warnings, each covering many high-risk buildings at once. Figure (d) counts how many hot-spot buildings the area rating would rank lower.

Why not plain Mann–Whitney or KS tests

  • Too many buildings: with 167,000 buildings, any tiny difference gives p ≈ 0, so a p-value says nothing about how large or important it is.
  • Not independent: buildings in the same subdistrict share its SEVI and flood together; plain tests treat them as independent and overstate certainty.
  • Used instead: effect sizes (how large), intervals from resampling whole subdistricts (how certain), and a test that shuffles the flooded label only inside subdistricts (the within part).

Two ways a flood could single out vulnerable buildings

  • Finding: Extent: if the flood holds a larger share of vulnerable buildings than the whole basin, ρ is above 1. Depth: a large subdistrict collects more flooded km², so it gets a higher hazard class even when the water is no deeper.
  • Why it matters: Subdistrict hazard partly measures size, so a link between subdistrict hazard and vulnerability has to be checked with size held fixed.

The highest hazard sits in large subdistricts

  • Subdistricts: subdistrict hazard ranks damage-weighted flooded area in km², so it rises with size (rank correlation 0.85); all 19 subdistricts in class 5 are larger than 10 km². These large subdistricts are less vulnerable (mean SEVI 0.38 vs 0.68), so hazard vs vulnerability is −0.51, but −0.09 with size held fixed.
  • Buildings: of the 5,535 buildings in the highest building hazard class, 4,920 (89 %) are in the 36 subdistricts larger than 10 km². There only 27 % are in vulnerability classes 4–5, against 43 % of hazard-5 buildings in small subdistricts. Inside single subdistricts there is no relation (median rank correlation −0.02, 74 subdistricts).
  • Why it matters: higher hazard looks linked to lower vulnerability mostly because of where it happens, not because floods avoid vulnerable people; the risk rating must combine the two.

Why all exposed buildings

  • Pool = 27,804 buildings in the flood extent (not all 166,999).
  • Easy to get: building footprints × flood extent; no risk model needed.
  • Missing at subdistrict level: each building's own H, E and V.
  • So: the three approaches differ only in building-level risk information.

Random pick in the last subdistrict

  • Problem: the budget ends inside a subdistrict. At N = 1,000, Suwan + Geonguk use 828 places, so 172 are left for Daechon (1,104 buildings).
  • Random pick: no building information, so each Daechon building has the same chance, p = 172 / 1,104 = 15.6 %.
  • Expected value: targets taken from Daechon = p × its targets.
\[\frac{m}{n_L}\times T_L=\frac{172}{1{,}104}\times 202=31.5\]m = places left, nL = buildings, TL = targets in the last subdistrict. Same share for residents.
  • Result: 301 + 31.5 = 332.5 targets → capture 6.3 %, precision 33.2 %.
  • Range: riskiest first 9.0 %, least risky first 5.7 % (not used: needs building risk).
